## Goals for this section

-   Add many predictors
-   Be able to interpret and visualize MR
-   Know how to do factorial ANOVA models
-   Be able to model, interpret, and visualize interactions

## Moving to many predictors

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
library(brms)
library(modelr)
library(patchwork)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidybayes)

# normal density
p1 <-
  tibble(x = seq(from = -3, to = 3, by = .1)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = (dnorm(x)) / max(dnorm(x)))) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "steelblue4", color = "steelblue4", alpha = .6) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = 0, y = .2,
           label = "normal",
           size = 7) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = c(0, 1.5), y = .6,
           label = c("italic(M)[0]", "italic(S)[0]"), 
           size = 7, family = "Times", parse = T) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.line.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.5))

# a second normal density
p2 <-
  tibble(x = seq(from = -3, to = 3, by = .1)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = (dnorm(x)) / max(dnorm(x)))) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "steelblue4", color = "steelblue4", alpha = .6) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = 0, y = .2,
           label = "normal",
           size = 7) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = c(0, 1.5), y = .6,
           label = c("italic(M)[italic(j)]", "italic(S)[italic(j)]"), 
           size = 7, family = "Times", parse = T) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.line.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.5))

## two annotated arrows
# save our custom arrow settings
my_arrow <- arrow(angle = 20, length = unit(0.35, "cm"), type = "closed")
p3 <-
  tibble(x    = c(.33, 1.67),
         y    = c(1, 1),
         xend = c(.67, 1.2),
         yend = c(0, 0)) %>%
  
  ggplot(aes(x = x, xend = xend,
             y = y, yend = yend)) +
  geom_segment(arrow = my_arrow) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
  x = c(.35, 1.3), y = .5,
  label = "'~'",
  size = 10, family = "Times", parse = T) +
  xlim(0, 2) +
  theme_void()

# likelihood formula
p5 <-
  tibble(x = .5,
         y = .25,
         label = "beta[0]+sum()[italic(j)]*beta[italic(j)]*italic(x)[italic(ji)]") %>% 
  
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label)) +
  geom_text(size = 7, parse = T, family = "Times") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  ylim(0, 1) +
  theme_void()
  
# exponential density (prior on sigma)
p6 <-
  tibble(x = seq(from = 0, to = 3, by = .01)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = (dexp(x, 1.5)) / max(dexp(x, 1.5)))) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "steelblue4", color = "steelblue4", alpha = .6) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = 1.5, y = .2,
           label = "exponential",
           size = 7) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = 1.5, y = .6,
           label = "italic(L)[sigma]", 
           size = 7, family = "Times", parse = T) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.line.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.5))

# two annotated arrows: mu's equation and sigma's prior feed the likelihood
p7 <-
  tibble(x    = c(1.5, 2.5),
         y    = c(1, 1),
         xend = c(1.5, 1.75),
         yend = c(.2, .2)) %>%
  
  ggplot(aes(x = x, xend = xend,
             y = y, yend = yend)) +
  geom_segment(arrow = my_arrow) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = c(1.38, 2), y = c(.65, .6),
           label = c("'='", "'~'"),
           size = 10, family = "Times", parse = T) +
  xlim(0, 3) +
  theme_void()

# normal likelihood
p8 <-
  tibble(x = seq(from = -3, to = 3, by = .1)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = (dnorm(x) / max(dnorm(x))))) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "steelblue4", color = "steelblue4", alpha = .6) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = 0, y = .2,
           label = "normal",
           size = 7) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = 0, y = .6,
           label = "mu[italic(i)]~~~sigma",
           size = 7, family = "Times", parse = T) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.line.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.5))

# the final annotated arrow
p9 <-
  tibble(x     = c(.375, .625),
         y     = c(1/3, 1/3),
         label = c("'~'", "italic(i)")) %>%

  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label)) +
  geom_text(size = c(10, 7), parse = T, family = "Times") +
  geom_segment(x = .5, xend = .5,
               y = 1, yend = 0,
               arrow = my_arrow) +
  xlim(0, 1) +
  theme_void()

# some text
p10 <-
  tibble(x     = .5,
         y     = .5,
         label = "italic(y[i])") %>% 
  
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label)) +
  geom_text(size = 7, parse = T, family = "Times") +
  xlim(0, 1) +
  theme_void()

# define the layout
layout <- c(
  area(t = 1, b = 2, l = 3, r = 5),
  area(t = 1, b = 2, l = 7, r = 9),
  area(t = 4, b = 5, l = 5, r = 7),
  area(t = 4, b = 5, l = 9, r = 11),
  area(t = 3, b = 4, l = 3, r = 9),
  area(t = 7, b = 8, l = 5, r = 7),
  area(t = 6, b = 7, l = 1, r = 11),
  area(t = 9, b = 9, l = 5, r = 7),
  area(t = 10, b = 10, l = 5, r = 7)
)

# combine and plot!
(p1 + p2 + p5 + p6 + p3 + p8 + p7 + p9 + p10) + 
  plot_layout(design = layout) &
  ylim(0, 1) &
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0, 5.5, 0, 5.5))
```

## Your turn: write the equation

Can you write this model equation? Assume two IVs.

## data

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| 
MR <- read.csv("hw3.csv")   # also at https://josh-jackson.github.io/bayes27/hw3.csv
MR <- MR %>% 
  mutate(SS_c = `schoool.success` - mean(`schoool.success`),
         FQ_c = `friendship.quality` - mean(`friendship.quality`),
         iv = `intervention.group`) %>% 
        mutate(iv = as.factor(iv))

MR <- MR %>%
  mutate(iv.d = factor(if_else(iv == "1", "control", "tx")))   # groups 2 and 3 are both treatment

MR
```

## Describing the data

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
library(psych)
describe(MR)
```

## model

$$\text{happiness}_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)$$
$$\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{SS}_i + \beta_2 \text{FQ}_i$$

$$\beta_0 \sim \text{Normal}(5, 2) \qquad \beta_1, \beta_2 \sim \text{Normal}(0, 2)$$
$$\sigma \sim \text{Exponential}(1)$$

SS (school success) and FQ (friendship quality) are both centered.

## Fitting the model

```{r}
mr.1 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 1 + SS_c + FQ_c,
      prior = c(prior(normal(5, 2), class = Intercept),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = SS_c),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = FQ_c),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, cores = 2,
      data = MR,
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      sample_prior = "yes",
      file = "mr.1")
```

## Equivalent notation

```{r, eval=FALSE}

                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, cores = 2,
      data = MR,
      sample_prior = "yes",
      backend = "cmdstanr",

```

## Prior predictive checks

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
prior.mr1 %>% 
  slice_sample(n = 100) %>% 
  rownames_to_column("draw") %>% 
  expand(nesting(draw, Intercept, b_SS_c),
         a = c(-10, 10)) %>% 
  mutate(d = Intercept + b_SS_c * a) %>% 
  
  ggplot(aes(x = a, y = d)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = draw), alpha = .4) +
  labs(x = "Centered School Success",
       y = "happiness") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 10)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) 
```

## tighter priors?

Slopes tightened from Normal(0, 2) to Normal(0, 0.2). (σ's prior changes too: Exponential(0.5) has mean 2, so it is a bit *looser*.)

```{r}

mr.2 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 1 + SS_c + FQ_c,
      prior = c(prior(normal(5, 2), class = Intercept),
                prior(normal(0, .2), class = b, coef = SS_c),
                prior(normal(0, .2), class = b, coef = FQ_c),
                prior(exponential(.5), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, cores = 2,
      data = MR,
      sample_prior = "yes",
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "mr.2")
```

## Are the predictors redundant? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.5
pairs(mr.1, variable = c("b_SS_c", "b_FQ_c"))
```

School success and friendship quality correlate −0.55 in the data, so their slopes are tied together in the posterior (correlation ≈ +0.55): when a draw gives SS more credit, it gives FQ more too, to explain the same variance. Correlated, but not redundant; truly redundant predictors make a long, thin ridge (lecture 5).

## Predictions across friendship quality

```{r}
library(marginaleffects)
plot_predictions(mr.1, condition = "FQ_c")
```

## Conditional plots

-   Remember, anytime we have a multiple regression we are working with a 3d (or higher) response plane (in frequentist land), and in Bayesian we are working with a hyperdimensional mountain.

-   Regardless of what estimation we are using, we need to communicate our effects in simple terms, usually by restricting to only one variable at a time.

-   To do so, we need to either average across or pick a point on the other variables in the model to visualize our effect of interest

## Two categorical predictors: a 2 × 3 study {.smaller}

Does how you study matter, and does it depend on sleep? (Simulated, so we know the truth.) Students either **re-read** their notes or take **practice tests**, and slept **4, 6, or 8 hours** the night before. Outcome: exam score (0–100). The cells are unequal: practice-testers tended to sleep more.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
set.seed(2027)
exam <- tibble(strategy = rep(c("reread", "practice"), each = 3),
               sleep    = rep(c("4h", "6h", "8h"), times = 2),
               n        = c(25, 30, 25, 15, 30, 35),
               true     = c(66, 70, 72, 67, 77, 84)) %>%    # true cell means
  uncount(n) %>%
  mutate(score    = pmin(rnorm(n(), true, 8), 100),
         strategy = factor(strategy, levels = c("reread", "practice")),
         sleep    = factor(sleep)) %>%
  select(-true)

exam %>% count(strategy, sleep) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = sleep, values_from = n)
```

## Three ways to code two factors {.smaller}

| Formula | Parameters | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `score ~ strategy + sleep` | a baseline + differences; no interaction | the strategy effect is the same at every sleep level |
| `score ~ strategy * sleep` | a baseline cell + differences + interaction terms | the usual factorial model |
| `score ~ 0 + strategy:sleep` | one mean per cell (index coding) | you want cell means directly, with one prior |

Why not one index per factor (`0 + strategy + sleep`)? `0 +` only removes one intercept, so the second factor is still dummy coded. And two separate index variables (as in Statistical Rethinking) aren't identified: add 1 to every strategy mean and subtract 1 from every sleep mean and the predictions don't change.

**Rule of thumb:** index coding for one factor, or for all the cells. Otherwise use the default coding and read results through predictions and contrasts, not coefficients.

## The factorial model, in brms's names {.smaller}

$$\text{score}_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)$$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_i = \beta_0 &+ \beta_1\,\text{practice}_i + \beta_2\,\text{sleep6h}_i + \beta_3\,\text{sleep8h}_i \\
&+ \beta_4\,(\text{practice} \times \text{sleep6h})_i + \beta_5\,(\text{practice} \times \text{sleep8h})_i
\end{aligned}
$$

$$\beta_0 \sim \text{Normal}(70, 10) \qquad \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_5 \sim \text{Normal}(0, 10) \qquad \sigma \sim \text{Exponential}(0.1)$$

Each name is a 0/1 dummy, as it appears in `summary()`. A typical exam average is around 70, differences beyond ±20 points would be surprising, and σ has a mean of 10 points. (brms puts the intercept prior at the average of the predictors, roughly the overall mean, so 70 works either way.)

## Fitting the factorial model

```{r}
fac.1 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      score ~ strategy * sleep,
      prior = c(prior(normal(70, 10), class = Intercept),
                prior(normal(0, 10), class = b),
                prior(exponential(.1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
      data = exam,
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "fac.1")
```

## What each coefficient means {.smaller}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
round(fixef(fac.1), 1)
```

| Coefficient | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Intercept` | the reference cell: re-read, 4 h |
| `strategypractice` | practice − re-read, **at 4 h only** |
| `sleep6h`, `sleep8h` | 6 h (8 h) − 4 h, **for re-readers only** |
| `strategypractice:sleep6h` (`…8h`) | how much bigger the practice advantage is at 6 h (8 h) than at 4 h |

Every coefficient is a difference from the reference cell; none is a "main effect." That's why we interpret factorial models through predictions.

## Cell means, two ways {.smaller}

By hand (practice, 8 h): add the coefficients that are "on" for that cell, draw by draw.

```{r}
fac.1 %>% 
  spread_draws(b_Intercept, b_strategypractice, b_sleep8h, `b_strategypractice:sleep8h`) %>% 
  mutate(practice_8h = b_Intercept + b_strategypractice + b_sleep8h + `b_strategypractice:sleep8h`) %>% 
  median_qi(practice_8h)
```

All six at once:

```{r}
avg_predictions(fac.1, by = c("strategy", "sleep"))
```

## marginaleffects: what it does by default {.smaller}

From here on, {marginaleffects} is our main tool for contrasts and slopes. It makes choices for you; know them:

-   **The grid.** With no `newdata`, it makes a prediction for *every row of your data*. `avg_*()` then **averages** those, e.g. averaging over the observed mix of groups. Not the same as a "typical" person (`newdata = "mean"`) or all factor combinations equally (`newdata = "balanced"`); a few slides on, two grids give two answers.
-   **The summary.** For a brms model, `estimate` is the posterior **median**, and the interval is equal-tailed (quantile) at 95%.
-   **The scale.** `type = "response"` (the default) vs. `"link"`. It doesn't matter yet, but it will for logistic and count models.
-   **The escape hatch.** `get_draws()` turns any result back into one row per draw, so you can check it by hand or plot it with tidybayes.

## The interaction, plotted {.smaller .nostretch}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 8
#| out-width: "90%"
avg_predictions(fac.1, by = c("sleep", "strategy")) %>% 
  get_draws() %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = sleep, y = draw, colour = strategy)) +
  geom_point(data = exam, aes(y = score), alpha = .25, size = 1.2,
             position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = .15, dodge.width = .5)) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = strategy), fun = median, geom = "line", position = position_dodge(width = .5)) +
  stat_pointinterval(position = position_dodge(width = .5), .width = .95) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(reread = "grey35", practice = "#D55E00"),
                      labels = c(reread = "re-read", practice = "practice tests")) +
  labs(x = "Sleep the night before", y = "Exam score", colour = NULL,
       caption = "Points: students. Dots and bars: posterior medians and 95% intervals for each cell mean.") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The lines aren't parallel: that's the interaction. This is the kind of figure HW 4 Q6a asks for.

## Simple effects, then the interaction {.smaller}

The practice-test advantage **at each sleep level** (simple effects):

```{r}
avg_comparisons(fac.1, variables = "strategy", by = "sleep")
```

Does that advantage **differ** across sleep levels? Differences between the simple effects *are* the interaction:

```{r}
avg_comparisons(fac.1, variables = "strategy", by = "sleep", hypothesis = ~ pairwise)
```

(In the simulation, the true advantages are 1, 7, and 12 points.)

## "Main effects" depend on the grid {.smaller}

Practice vs. re-read, ignoring sleep. Two reasonable grids, two answers:

```{r}
avg_predictions(fac.1, by = "strategy", hypothesis = ~ pairwise)                        # each group's own sleep mix
avg_predictions(fac.1, by = "strategy", newdata = "balanced", hypothesis = ~ pairwise)  # 4, 6, 8 h weighted equally
```

Practice-testers slept more, so the first comparison mixes the strategy effect with the sleep effect. The balanced grid compares them at the same sleep mix. With an interaction, *any* single "main effect" is an average over some grid: say which one.

## Each cell: the mean vs. a new person {.smaller .nostretch}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 9
#| out-width: "100%"
cell_grid <- datagrid(model = fac.1, strategy = unique, sleep = unique)
bind_rows("cell mean (epred)"        = predictions(fac.1, newdata = cell_grid) %>% get_draws(),
          "a new person (prediction)" = predictions(fac.1, newdata = cell_grid, type = "prediction") %>% get_draws(),
          .id = "interval") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = draw, y = sleep, colour = interval)) +
  stat_pointinterval(position = position_dodge(width = .5), .width = .95) +
  facet_wrap(~ strategy) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("cell mean (epred)" = "#0072B2", "a new person (prediction)" = "grey55")) +
  labs(x = "Exam score (95% intervals)", y = "Sleep", colour = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The cell-mean interval is our uncertainty about the *average* in that cell; it shrinks as the cell gets more people. The prediction interval adds σ, the person-to-person scatter, so it stays wide no matter how much data we have. (HW 4 Q2b.)

## Cell-means coding gives the same cells {.smaller}

Index coding with one mean per cell, and one prior for all six:

```{r}
fac.2 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      score ~ 0 + strategy:sleep,
      prior = c(prior(normal(70, 10), class = b),
                prior(exponential(.1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
      data = exam,
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "fac.2")
round(fixef(fac.2)[, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")], 1)
```

Essentially the same six cell means as `fac.1` (the priors differ slightly), read straight off the output. Differences and interaction contrasts work exactly as before with marginaleffects.

## Interactions: a slope with its own equation {.smaller}

An interaction means the effect of one variable depends on another. In toolbox terms (lecture 3): **the slope gets its own equation.**

$$\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_{1i} X_i + \beta_2 Z_i \qquad \beta_{1i} = \beta_1 + \beta_3 Z_i$$

Substitute and you get the familiar $\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \beta_2 Z_i + \beta_3 X_i Z_i$.

-   $\beta_1$ is now the slope of X **when Z = 0** (why centering Z matters)
-   $\beta_3$ is how much the slope of X changes for each unit of Z
-   With an interaction there's no single "main effect" of X: describe the slope of X *at chosen values of Z* (or the group difference at chosen values of X)

The modeling is the easy part; interpreting is the work, and predictions, `slopes()`, and plots do most of it.

## Nominal plus metric/continuous interaction

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

  brm(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 0 + iv.d + SS_c,
      prior = c(prior(normal(5, 3), class = b, coef = iv.dcontrol),
                prior(normal(5, 3), class = b, coef = iv.dtx),
                prior(normal(0, .5), class = b, coef = SS_c),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
      data = MR, 
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "mr.12")
```

## Three groups × a continuous predictor

The same idea with all three intervention groups and a continuous moderator (SES). With three groups, the "effect of SES" is three slopes, and the interaction asks whether they differ. This is where marginaleffects saves a lot of hand computation.

```{r}
a.4 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 1 + iv*SES,
      prior = c(prior(normal(5, 3), class = Intercept),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, cores = 2,
      data = MR,
      sample_prior = "yes",
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "a.4b")

```

## Fitting the interaction model

```{r}
mr.15 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 1 + SS_c * FQ_c,
      prior = c(prior(normal(5, 2), class = Intercept),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = SS_c),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = FQ_c),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = SS_c:FQ_c),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, cores = 2,
      data = MR,
      sample_prior = "yes",
       backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "mr.15b")
```

## Interaction results

```{r}
summary(mr.15)
```

## The model is a surface {.smaller .nostretch}

Two continuous predictors make a surface. Without an interaction the contours would be straight and parallel; the interaction bends them.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-width: 7
#| out-width: "80%"
predictions(mr.15, newdata = datagrid(SS_c = seq(min(MR$SS_c), max(MR$SS_c), length.out = 60),
                                      FQ_c = seq(min(MR$FQ_c), max(MR$FQ_c), length.out = 60))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = SS_c, y = FQ_c, z = estimate)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = estimate)) +
  geom_contour(colour = "white", bins = 8) +
  geom_point(data = MR, aes(x = SS_c, y = FQ_c), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 1, alpha = .6) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = "school success (centered)", y = "friendship quality (centered)", fill = "predicted\nhappiness") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13)
```

## Reading the interaction coefficients {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
b15 <- fixef(mr.15)[, "Estimate"]
```

-   **`SS_c` = `r sprintf("%.2f", b15["SS_c"])`:** the slope of school success **when FQ_c = 0**, i.e., at average friendship quality (centering made 0 meaningful)
-   **`SS_c:FQ_c` = `r sprintf("%.2f", b15["SS_c:FQ_c"])`:** each extra point of friendship quality changes the SS slope by that much
-   So at FQ_c = −2.5 and +2.5 (about ±1 SD), the SS slope is `r sprintf("%.2f", b15["SS_c"] - 2.5 * b15["SS_c:FQ_c"])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", b15["SS_c"] + 2.5 * b15["SS_c:FQ_c"])`: school success matters more for people with weaker friendships
-   Uncentered, the `SS` coefficient would be its slope at friendship quality = 0, a value nobody in the data has

## Does the interaction add much? {.smaller}

Bayesian R² with and without the interaction (HW 4 Q5):

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
bind_rows("SS + FQ (mr.1)"         = as_tibble(bayes_R2(mr.1)),
          "SS × FQ (mr.15)"        = as_tibble(bayes_R2(mr.15)), .id = "model") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

A small gain, with heavily overlapping intervals. R² can only go up when you add terms, so it can't tell you whether the interaction is worth it; lecture 6 uses LOO for that.
